title: Secrets belong in the keychain
summary: Move credentials out of web storage, gate access with the platform keystore, and review a native token design.

scenario.briefing: The campus app stores its refresh token in localStorage, copies it into Preferences for the native shell, and logs it during sync failures. A lost phone should not hand over a session. Replace the storage path with the platform keystore and clear it on logout.

objectives.description: Identify credentials in web storage, logs, and plain preferences.
Explain keychain access control and credential lifecycle.

hints: localStorage and Preferences are readable by the app and its scripts.
Use Keychain on iOS and Keystore on Android through a secure storage plugin.
Require device authentication for sensitive reads when the platform supports it.
Clear the token on logout and never write it to logs.

misconceptions.description: Treating Capacitor Preferences as encrypted storage.
misconceptions.feedback: Preferences is convenience storage, not a credential vault. Use the platform Keychain or Keystore.

misconceptions.description: Logging a token to diagnose a sync failure.
misconceptions.feedback: Logs are copied, shipped, and retained. A token in a log is a live credential; log an error code instead.

misconceptions.description: Believing encryption at rest makes a credential safe to expose.
misconceptions.feedback: Encryption at rest protects a stolen disk, not a running app or a log. Access control and minimization still matter.

sections.title: Web storage is not a vault
sections.body: localStorage and sessionStorage are readable by any script in the page. Capacitor Preferences is a key-value store, not an encrypted credential store. A refresh token there is exposed to XSS and to anyone with file access.

sections.title: Use the platform keystore
sections.body: The iOS Keychain and Android Keystore protect credentials with OS access control. A Capacitor secure-storage plugin exposes them to the app. Request device authentication for high-value reads when the platform supports it.

sections.title: Credentials have a lifecycle
sections.body: Store only what the app needs, clear it on logout, rotate after suspicion, and never log it. Biometric gating is an access decision, not a replacement for revocation.

steps.title: Review the token storage
steps.prompt: Select every supported finding and choose a verdict.
hints: Find every place the token is written.
Check whether any of those places is encrypted by the OS.
Look at the sync error path.
Block the design: localStorage, Preferences, logs, and no biometric gate all expose the token.

findings.label: The refresh token is stored in localStorage.
A sync failure logs the refresh token.
Preferences stores the token in plain app storage, not the OS keystore.
A biometric flag in Preferences does not gate access to the token.
Preferences encrypts credentials with the device keystore.

verdicts.label: Block until the token uses the keystore and leaves logs and web storage

steps.explanation: The token is copied into two plain stores and a log. It belongs in the platform keystore with an access-control policy and no logging.

steps.title: Write the keystore adapter
steps.prompt: Edit storage.ts. saveToken, readToken, and clearToken must use the app's SecureStorage adapter, require device authentication for reads, clear the token on logout, and never log it.
hints: Import the secure storage plugin instead of Preferences or localStorage.
Set an access-control option that requires device authentication.
Log only an error code, never the token value.

localVerification.description: Runs the structural checks that exercise this storage adapter.

tests.description: Uses the platform secure storage plugin.

steps.title: Protect the credential lifecycle
hints: The OS keystore protects secrets better than a web store.
Logging a secret makes it persistent.
Biometric access is separate from revocation.
Select keystore storage, access control, logout clearing, and no logging; reject encryption as total safety.

statements.label: The Keychain and Keystore provide OS-level access control for credentials.
Logout should clear the stored token and revoke the session when possible.
Tokens must never be written to application logs.
Device authentication can gate a read but does not replace revocation.
Encryption at rest makes it safe to expose a token in logs.

steps.explanation: Credential safety combines OS-protected storage, access control, clearing on logout, revocation, and keeping secrets out of logs.
